label: Hyperbolic Geometry
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 483 through 504. We specialize the Cayley-Klein machinery to one nondegenerate real absolute, the unit circle, and let its interior become the hyperbolic plane. Stress that every metric notion to come, distance and angle alike, is read off the absolute conic by cross-ratios.

label: The Absolute Conic
notes: Introduce the quadratic form x squared plus y squared minus z squared. Interior points give negative values, boundary points vanish, exterior points are positive. The interior is the material hyperbolic plane; the boundary is ideal; the exterior is projective bookkeeping that keeps intersections alive. This sign test underlies everything else.

label: Beltrami-Klein Model
notes: Present the open unit disk with straight chords as geodesics. The big selling point is that incidence is linear, so joins and meets are ordinary projective operations. Note that two chords can fail to meet inside the disk while their projective lines still meet outside, which removes case distinctions.

label: Distance by Cross-Ratio
notes: Derive the Klein distance from the cross-ratio of P and Q with the two boundary points X and Y where their chord meets the circle. The one-half log absolute value form is forced by additivity and the requirement that ideal points sit infinitely far away. Emphasize projective invariance.

label: Many Parallels
notes: Contrast with Euclid. Through an outside point P there is a whole fan of chords missing a given line, bounded by two limiting parallels that share an ideal endpoint with the line. Everything between is ultraparallel. This visibly breaks the parallel postulate while keeping the other axioms.

label: Angle of Parallelism
notes: Define the angle of parallelism as the angle between the perpendicular dropped from a point and a limiting parallel. Lobachevsky's formula ties it to the distance from the point to the line. As distance grows the angle shrinks to zero, which is the quantitative signature of hyperbolic divergence.

label: Poincare Disk Model
notes: Switch to the conformal disk. Geodesics are circular arcs meeting the boundary orthogonally, and angles are ordinary Euclidean angles. The radial map relates the Poincare coordinate z to the Klein coordinate w. Same ideal boundary, different drawing, chosen so angle measurement becomes painless.

label: Upper Half-Plane
notes: Present the upper half-plane as a Mobius image of the disk. Geodesics are vertical lines and semicircles centered on the real axis, which is the ideal boundary. Mobius maps with real coefficients are the isometries. Useful because many computations linearize on the real boundary line.

label: Isometries
notes: State the unifying principle: hyperbolic isometries are exactly the projectivities preserving the absolute conic, equivalently the disk-preserving Mobius and anti-Mobius maps. The normal form sends a chosen point to the center with the boundary fixed, which is the standard trick for simplifying distance and angle calculations.

label: Triangles and Defect
notes: State the angle-sum theorem: every hyperbolic triangle has angle sum strictly less than pi. The defect, pi minus the sum, is positive and, by Gauss-Bonnet on a curvature minus-one surface, equals the area. Larger triangles are thinner; an ideal triangle has all angles zero and area pi.

label: Hyperbolic Trigonometry
notes: Replace circular functions with hyperbolic ones. Give the law of cosines with cosh of the sides and the law of sines using sinh. Note the AAA congruence consequence: angles determine a triangle up to isometry, because there is an absolute length scale set by the curvature.

label: Synthesis
notes: Recap the through-line. One real absolute conic generates the whole hyperbolic plane. The Klein model linearizes incidence, the Poincare and half-plane models linearize angles, and Mobius maps move between them. Distance and angle are cross-ratios, and isometries are the conic-preserving projectivities. Point to the notebook checks.
